subject: biology

items.q: Which of these changes would a biologist regard as evolution?
items.correct: The frequency of an allele for dark wing colour rises in a moth population over many generations.
items.misconception: The muscles a weightlifter enlarges by training are inherited by the weightlifter's children.
items.why: This is Lamarck's explanation, which is often taught as the historical alternative to Darwin's and matches the everyday intuition that parents 'pass on' whatever they have. Students also meet examples such as giraffes stretching their necks presented as if they were explanations rather than errors. Evolution is change in the heritable characteristics of a population. Acquired changes that are not genetic in origin are not inherited and are not regarded as evolution; only alleles present in gametes are passed to the next generation.
items.specStatementText: Evolution is heritable change in a population, and why it is still called a theory
items.random_wrong: An individual Arctic fox grows a thicker and whiter coat each year as winter approaches.

items.q: A student says: 'Evolution by natural selection is only a theory, so it has not been proved and could easily be overturned.' Which response best evaluates this claim?
items.correct: The theory cannot be formally proved true, but it predicts and explains so many observations that it is unlikely ever to be falsified.
items.misconception: The claim is wrong because the theory has been proved true by direct observation of every prediction that it makes.
items.why: School science is often presented as establishing facts, and 'proof' is used loosely for any convincing evidence, so students expect a strongly supported theory to have been proved. A theory can be falsified by an observation that contradicts it, but no finite set of confirming observations can prove it true for all cases. The theory of evolution is unlikely ever to be falsified and is therefore a pragmatic truth, which is why it is still called a theory.
items.specStatementText: Evolution is heritable change in a population, and why it is still called a theory
items.random_wrong: The claim is right: a scientific theory is just an untested idea, and evolution will become a fact once enough evidence has been gathered.

items.q: The amino acid sequence of the same protein was compared in four species. Compared with species W, species X differs at 2 positions, species Y at 15 positions and species Z at 31 positions. Which conclusion is supported by the data?
items.correct: W shares a more recent common ancestor with X than it does with either Y or Z.
items.misconception: Z is the most primitive of the four species, because its sequence is furthest from W's.
items.why: The ladder image of evolution, with humans at the top, leads students to read any comparison against a human sequence as a ranking rather than as a measure of time since divergence. Sequence differences accumulate in both lineages after they split from a common ancestor, so the number of differences between two species indicates how long ago they diverged, not which is more advanced. Sequence data is evidence of common ancestry, not of a ladder of progress.
items.specStatementText: Sequence similarity is evidence of common ancestry
items.random_wrong: X lives in the same kind of habitat as W, because similar conditions give similar proteins.

items.q: For one gene, two species have identical amino acid sequences in the protein, yet the base sequences of the gene differ at six positions. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: Some base substitutions leave the amino acid that is coded for unchanged.
items.misconception: They are not evidence of divergence, because they have had no effect on the protein.
items.why: Students define evolution by visible change and by the action of natural selection on phenotypes, so a difference with no phenotypic effect looks like 'nothing happened'. Base sequences in DNA or RNA are themselves evidence for evolution: differences accumulate over time after lineages split, including differences that leave the amino acid sequence unchanged, and their number reflects the time since the common ancestor.
items.specStatementText: Sequence similarity is evidence of common ancestry
items.random_wrong: The genes must actually be identical, so the six differences are sequencing errors.

items.q: Cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and Brussels sprouts were all produced from wild cabbage (Brassica oleracea) by selective breeding over the past few thousand years. What does this show about evolution?
items.correct: The heritable characteristics of a population can change greatly in a short time when selection is strong.
items.misconception: Breeders were able to produce each new characteristic by causing the mutation that was needed for it.
items.why: 'Breeding for' a feature sounds like manufacturing it, and students rarely see that the raw material is variation that already exists, including chance mutations that the breeder did not cause. Selective breeding works by choosing which individuals reproduce from the heritable variation already present. The breeder cannot cause a particular mutation; selection changes the frequency of alleles that exist in the population.
items.specStatementText: Selective breeding shows how fast heritable change can happen
items.random_wrong: It is not evidence of evolution, because the changes were brought about by humans rather than by nature.

items.q: The arm of a human, the wing of a bat and the flipper of a whale are used for grasping, flying and swimming, yet each has one upper bone, two lower bones, a group of wrist bones and five digits. Why is this evidence for evolution?
items.correct: The shared bone pattern was inherited from a common ancestor and has been modified for different functions.
items.misconception: Five digits is the best possible arrangement for any limb, so each of the species evolved the pattern separately.
items.why: Students are used to explaining structures by their function, and it seems natural that the best design would be reached independently, as it is for analogous structures. The pentadactyl pattern is not required by function: a paddle or a wing could be built in many ways, and a whale has no use for separate digits. The shared pattern is explained by inheritance from a common ancestor, which is why homologous structures are evidence for evolution.
items.specStatementText: Homologous structures share an origin, not a function
items.random_wrong: The limbs are analogous structures, which show that different functions evolve from different origins.

items.q: Sharks, which are fish, and dolphins, which are mammals, both have streamlined bodies, a dorsal fin and paddle-shaped front fins. Which statement about these features is correct?
items.correct: They are analogous: they evolved separately because similar selection favoured similar shapes in water.
items.misconception: They are homologous, showing that dolphins are more closely related to sharks than they are to other mammals.
items.why: Prior classification work groups organisms by visible similarity, and everyday categories such as 'fish' are based on shape and habitat, so students read any resemblance as kinship. Analogous structures have the same function but different evolutionary origins. Relatedness is shown by homologous structures and sequence data, not by features that convergent evolution can produce independently.
items.specStatementText: Analogous structures come from convergent evolution
items.random_wrong: They are homologous, because in both animals the features perform the same function in water.

items.q: Which of these is an example of speciation?
items.correct: A population splits into two groups that then become unable to interbreed with each other.
items.misconception: A species changes gradually over millions of years until it looks quite different from its ancestors.
items.why: Popular accounts describe one species 'evolving into' another, and the idea that enough change must eventually produce a new species seems obvious, so splitting is not recognized as the essential step. New species have appeared only by the splitting of pre-existing species. Gradual evolutionary change in a species is not speciation, because it produces no additional species.
items.specStatementText: New species only ever come from splitting old ones
items.random_wrong: A river splits a population into two halves, which are at once regarded as separate species.

items.q: Over a period of time, 40 speciation events and 25 extinctions were recorded in a group of organisms. Over the same period several other species in the group changed gradually without splitting. What happened to the number of species in the group?
items.correct: It rose by 15, because only the splitting of species adds to the total and only extinction removes from it.
items.misconception: It fell by 25, because each speciation changes an existing species rather than adding one.
items.why: If evolution is pictured as a chain of transformations rather than a branching tree, each speciation event appears to replace one species with another. Speciation is the splitting of a pre-existing species, so it increases the total number of species on Earth, while extinction decreases it. Only these two processes change the number of species.
items.specStatementText: New species only ever come from splitting old ones
items.random_wrong: It rose by more than 15, because the species that changed gradually also became new species.

items.q: Bonobos live south of the Congo River and common chimpanzees live north of it; neither species swims. How did the two species arise from one ancestral population?
items.correct: The river prevented interbreeding, and different selection pressures on each side caused the populations to diverge.
items.misconception: The river caused mutations to occur that made the apes on each side of it different from one another.
items.why: Explanations such as 'the population adapted to the cold' are heard as the environment acting on the population, and the two-step process of random mutation followed by selection is collapsed into a single directed change. Differential selection acts on variation that already exists in a population; it does not create it. Different selection pressures on the two sides of a barrier change allele frequencies in different directions, and this is what makes isolated populations diverge.
items.specStatementText: Isolation starts speciation; differential selection completes it
items.random_wrong: Apes on each side of the river developed the features they needed to survive there and passed them on to their offspring.

items.q: A population of lizards was split when rising sea level cut off an island from the mainland. Many generations later, island and mainland lizards can no longer produce fertile offspring together. Which statement about this speciation is correct?
items.correct: Separation stopped gene flow, so selection on each side could change the two gene pools independently.
items.misconception: Separation was enough by itself, and the two populations were different species as soon as they were cut off.
items.why: Speciation is often summarized as 'isolation leads to new species', so the divergence stage is skipped and the barrier is taken as the whole story. Speciation needs both reproductive isolation, which stops gene flow, and differential selection, which makes the isolated gene pools diverge. Bonobos and common chimpanzees became separate species because conditions on the two sides of the Congo River differed, not simply because the river was there.
items.specStatementText: Isolation starts speciation; differential selection completes it
items.random_wrong: The populations only became different species once the lizards began to look different from one another.

items.q: Two populations of a fly species live in the same orchard but lay their eggs on different fruit species, which ripen at different times, so the flies rarely mate with each other. Which type of speciation could this lead to, and why?
items.correct: Sympatric speciation, because temporal isolation is cutting gene flow with no geographical barrier.
items.misconception: Allopatric speciation, because the two kinds of fruit tree act as a geographical barrier between the populations.
items.why: Allopatric speciation is taught first and its mountain-range or river barrier becomes the template for all speciation, so students try to find a barrier in every example. Reproductive isolation can be geographic, behavioural or temporal. Sympatric speciation happens without a geographical barrier: populations in the same place stop interbreeding because of differences in courtship behaviour or in the timing of reproduction.
items.specStatementText: Allopatric and sympatric speciation
items.random_wrong: Neither, because temporal isolation refers to species that lived at different times in Earth's history.

items.q: What do allopatric speciation and sympatric speciation have in common?
items.correct: Both require reproductive isolation of the populations, so that their gene pools can diverge.
items.misconception: Both require the populations to live in separate areas at some stage in the process.
items.why: Students assume that animals mate with any available partner, so the only way to stop gene flow they can picture is physical separation. Reproductive isolation can be behavioural or temporal as well as geographic. Populations in the same area that respond only to their own courtship signals, or reproduce at different times, are reproductively isolated and can undergo sympatric speciation.
items.specStatementText: Allopatric and sympatric speciation
items.random_wrong: Both require a physical barrier, though in sympatric speciation the barrier is very small.

items.q: A single species of finch colonized a remote group of islands that had no other land birds. Its descendants now form many species, each with a beak suited to a different food. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: Vacant niches let the descendants diversify, and specializing on different foods lets the species coexist.
items.misconception: This is convergent evolution, because unrelated birds reaching the islands evolved similar beaks.
items.why: Both terms are met in the same topic and both involve adaptation, and 'radiation' is not obviously about spreading outwards, so the two are conflated. Adaptive radiation is divergent: descendants of one species spread out into different niches and become more different from each other. Convergent evolution is the opposite pattern, in which unrelated lineages come to resemble each other.
items.specStatementText: Adaptive radiation fills vacant niches
items.random_wrong: The finches developed the beaks they needed for each food and passed those beaks on to their offspring.

items.q: A horse has 64 chromosomes and a donkey has 62. A mule, their hybrid, is healthy and vigorous but almost always sterile. Why is the mule sterile?
items.correct: Its 63 chromosomes cannot all pair up during meiosis, so it does not form viable gametes.
items.misconception: It has only half of the horse's genes and half of the donkey's, so it lacks a complete set of instructions.
items.why: Students learn that gametes carry half the chromosomes and reason that a hybrid, made from two different halves, cannot add up to a complete organism. Each gamete carries a complete haploid set, so the hybrid has a full set from each parent species and develops normally. The two sets are not homologous, so they cannot pair in meiosis, and that is why the hybrid is sterile.
items.specStatementText: Barriers and sterile hybrids keep gene pools apart
items.random_wrong: Horses and donkeys must be the same species, so the sterility is a result of inbreeding.

items.q: Two closely related bird species live in the same forest. The males of each species sing a different song, and females respond only to the song of their own species. What is the significance of this for the two species?
items.correct: It prevents hybridization, so that alleles do not pass between the two gene pools.
items.misconception: It lets the two species coexist by preventing them from competing with each other for food.
items.why: The principle of competitive exclusion is remembered without its condition, which is that the species occupy the same niche, so all similar species are expected to compete intensely. Adaptive radiation allows closely related species to coexist without competing because each becomes adapted to a different niche. Competitive exclusion applies to species that need the same resources, not to related species that have specialized in different ways.
items.specStatementText: Barriers and sterile hybrids keep gene pools apart
items.random_wrong: It is not a barrier to hybridization, because only physical differences can stop two species breeding.

items.q: Suppose one Persicaria species has 20 chromosomes in each diploid cell and another has 24. A hybrid forms between them, and in one hybrid plant the chromosome number doubles. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The doubled plant has 44 chromosomes, can pair them all in meiosis, and is a new species isolated from both parents.
items.misconception: The doubled plant remains sterile, because its chromosomes still come from two different species.
items.why: Sterility is attributed to the species mixture itself rather than to the mechanical problem of pairing in meiosis, so changing the number of chromosomes seems irrelevant. Hybrid sterility arises because the chromosomes from the two species have no homologous partners to pair with. Polyploidy provides a partner for every chromosome, so meiosis proceeds and the plant is fertile; this is how many Persicaria species have formed.
items.specStatementText: Plants can form new species in one generation
items.random_wrong: The doubled plant is still the same species as its parents, because it can breed with either of them.

items.q: A botanist claims that species R of Persicaria arose abruptly by hybridization between species P and species Q, followed by polyploidy. Which observation would best support this claim?
items.correct: The diploid chromosome number of R equals the diploid numbers of species P and Q added together.
items.misconception: R appears in the fossil record after a long series of intermediate forms between P and Q.
items.why: Speciation is usually taught through allopatric examples in which isolated populations diverge slowly, so gradual divergence is taken to be the only route. Abrupt speciation occurs in plants by hybridization and polyploidy. The polyploid hybrid is fertile with itself but not with either parent species, so a new species exists within one generation, as in the knotweeds and smartweeds of the genus Persicaria.
items.specStatementText: Plants can form new species in one generation
items.random_wrong: R produces fully fertile offspring when crossed with either species P or species Q.

items.q: An Arctic fox grows a thicker white coat each winter. Is the fox evolving?
items.correct: No. The change is a response by an individual during its lifetime and is not a change in the heritable characteristics of the population, so it is not evolution.
items.misconception: An individual organism evolves when it changes or adapts to its surroundings during its own lifetime.
items.why: In everyday language 'adapt' and 'evolve' are used for any change an individual makes, and in fiction organisms 'evolve' new features on the spot, so the population-level, multi-generational meaning of evolution is not the one students bring. Individuals do not evolve; populations do. Evolution is a change across generations in the heritable characteristics of a population, whereas changes in an individual's body during its life are acquired and are not passed on.
items.specStatementText: Evolution is heritable change in a population, and why it is still called a theory
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A new feeding technique spreads through a chimpanzee group as young animals copy adults. Is this evolution?
items.correct: No. Learned behaviour is passed on by teaching and imitation, not through alleles in gametes, so it is not a heritable characteristic in the genetic sense and its spread is not evolution.
items.misconception: Any change that is passed on from one generation to the next, including learned skills and traditions, counts as a change in heritable characteristics and so is evolution.
items.why: 'Heritable' is easily read as 'handed down', and cultural transmission is handed down from parents to offspring, so students treat learning that spreads through a population as if it were genetic inheritance. In the definition of evolution, heritable characteristics are those determined by alleles passed on in gametes. Behaviour learned during life is an acquired characteristic, not genetic in origin, so its spread through a population is not evolution.
items.specStatementText: Evolution is heritable change in a population, and why it is still called a theory
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the theory of evolution be tested, given that it concerns events in the past?
items.correct: Yes. The theory makes predictions about what should be observed in the present, for example in sequence data, homologous structures and selective breeding, and these predictions can be tested and could in principle falsify it.
items.misconception: Evolution cannot be tested scientifically because it concerns events that happened in the past and nobody was there to observe them.
items.why: Students equate scientific testing with laboratory experiments on events as they happen, and the claim that 'no one saw it' is a common argument they encounter outside school. A theory is tested by the predictions it makes, not only by direct observation of past events. The theory of evolution by natural selection predicts and explains a broad range of present-day observations, and this is why it is unlikely ever to be falsified.
items.specStatementText: Evolution is heritable change in a population, and why it is still called a theory
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Human and chimpanzee DNA base sequences are very similar. Does this mean that chimpanzees are the ancestors of humans?
items.correct: No. Both are living species descended from a common ancestral population that no longer exists; the similarity shows that the two lineages split recently, not that one species gave rise to the other.
items.misconception: When two living species have very similar sequences, the one regarded as simpler or older is the ancestor of the other.
items.why: Popular images of evolution as a line of figures from ape to human, and phrases such as 'humans evolved from monkeys', present living species as stages in a ladder rather than as branch tips of a tree. Sequence data gives evidence of common ancestry: species with few differences share a recent common ancestor. Neither living species is the ancestor of the other; both have been evolving separately since their lineages split.
items.specStatementText: Sequence similarity is evidence of common ancestry
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two species have an identical amino acid sequence for a protein. Must the base sequences of the gene be identical too?
items.correct: No. Because the genetic code is degenerate, several codons specify the same amino acid, so base substitutions can occur without changing the amino acid sequence; the gene sequences can differ while the protein is identical.
items.misconception: Every change in the base sequence of a gene changes the protein it codes for, so an identical protein means an identical gene.
items.why: Mutation is introduced with examples that change the protein, such as sickle cell anaemia, and the one-gene-one-protein idea is remembered as a one-to-one match between bases and amino acids. Several different codons code for the same amino acid, so some base substitutions leave the amino acid sequence unchanged. This is why base sequences usually reveal more differences between species than the amino acid sequences of their proteins, and give a finer measure of relatedness.
items.specStatementText: Sequence similarity is evidence of common ancestry
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Dog breeds were produced by human selection rather than by natural selection. Is the variation between breeds evidence for evolution?
items.correct: Yes. Selective breeding changed the heritable characteristics of populations, which is evolution by definition; that the selection was done by humans does not alter what changed, and it shows how rapidly heritable characteristics can change under selection.
items.misconception: Selective breeding is not evolution and is not evidence for it, because the changes were made by humans rather than occurring naturally.
items.why: Evolution is taught alongside natural selection, so students treat 'natural' as part of the definition and regard anything caused by humans as artificial and outside biology. Evolution is change in the heritable characteristics of a population, whatever the source of the selection. Variation between domesticated breeds and varieties, and between them and the original wild species, shows how rapidly evolutionary change can occur when selection is strong.
items.specStatementText: Selective breeding shows how fast heritable change can happen
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are a Chihuahua and a Great Dane members of different species?
items.correct: No. All domestic dog breeds belong to a single species; they differ in heritable characteristics because of selective breeding, but they are not reproductively isolated.
items.misconception: Domesticated breeds and crop varieties that look very different from one another are separate species.
items.why: Students judge species by appearance, and the visible differences between breeds or between cabbage and cauliflower are far larger than those between many genuine species. Breeds and varieties are populations of one species that differ because of selective breeding. Their variation shows how rapidly evolutionary change can occur, but a new species arises only when populations become reproductively isolated and can no longer interbreed.
items.specStatementText: Selective breeding shows how fast heritable change can happen
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What makes two structures homologous?
items.correct: Descent from the same structure in a common ancestor, shown by a shared underlying pattern; homologous structures may now perform different functions, as the pentadactyl limbs of humans, bats and whales do.
items.misconception: Homologous structures are ones that perform the same function, and analogous structures are ones that share the same origin.
items.why: The two terms are learned as a pair of near-identical words and the definitions are swapped; 'homo-' is not connected to 'same origin' and 'analogous' in everyday use means 'doing the same job'. Homologous structures share an origin in a common ancestor and are evidence for evolution because the same pattern has been modified for different functions. Analogous structures have the same function but different evolutionary origins, and arise by convergent evolution.
items.specStatementText: Homologous structures share an origin, not a function
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Sharks and dolphins have evolved similar streamlined shapes. Are they becoming more closely related?
items.correct: No. Convergent evolution produces similar features in separate lineages; the two species remain as distantly related as before and do not merge.
items.misconception: Convergent evolution means that two species are converging towards each other and will eventually become more closely related or merge into one species.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'converge' is to come together, so students picture the lineages themselves meeting rather than only their features becoming similar. Convergent evolution is the independent evolution of similar features in unrelated lineages under similar selection pressures. It is the origin of analogous structures; relatedness is fixed by ancestry and cannot change.
items.specStatementText: Analogous structures come from convergent evolution
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the number of species on Earth kept constant, with each new species balanced by an extinction?
items.correct: No. Speciation increases the number of species and extinction decreases it independently; when they are unequal the number of species changes, as it has through Earth's history.
items.misconception: Nature keeps the number of species in balance, so every speciation is matched by an extinction and the total stays the same.
items.why: Ecology is taught with equilibrium ideas such as balanced populations and stable ecosystems, and students extend 'balance of nature' to the number of species itself. The number of species is the outcome of two separate processes: speciation, which increases it, and extinction, which decreases it. There is no mechanism that balances them, and the number of species has both risen and fallen over geological time.
items.specStatementText: New species only ever come from splitting old ones
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are two populations different species once they look different from each other?
items.correct: No. Populations are separate species when they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring; appearance may differ within one species and may stay similar between two species.
items.misconception: Two populations become separate species when they look different, and remain one species as long as they look alike.
items.why: Species are first learned as kinds of organism recognized by their appearance, and field guides and classification keys reinforce a purely visual criterion. The test for speciation is reproductive isolation: separate species cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Divergence in appearance often accompanies this but is neither necessary nor sufficient.
items.specStatementText: Isolation starts speciation; differential selection completes it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is temporal isolation?
items.correct: Reproductive isolation caused by differences in the timing of reproduction, such as breeding in different seasons or flowering at different times, between populations living in the same area.
items.misconception: Temporal isolation means that two groups lived at different times in Earth's history and so could not meet.
items.why: 'Temporal' is met in the sense of geological time, and species that lived in different eras obviously cannot interbreed, so the term is attached to the wrong idea. Temporal isolation is one way present-day populations sharing an area can be reproductively isolated: if they mate, flower or spawn at different times, alleles cannot pass between them, and this can lead to sympatric speciation.
items.specStatementText: Allopatric and sympatric speciation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a mule. Does this mean that horses and donkeys are the same species?
items.correct: No. The mule is almost always sterile, so no alleles pass between the horse and donkey gene pools; the ability to produce a sterile hybrid does not make two populations one species.
items.misconception: Any two organisms that can mate and produce offspring belong to the same species.
items.why: The species definition is often learned in a shortened form, 'organisms that can breed together', which drops the requirement for fertile offspring. Members of a species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Interspecific hybrids such as the mule are sterile, which is a mechanism that prevents the mixing of alleles between species, so the parent species remain distinct.
items.specStatementText: Barriers and sterile hybrids keep gene pools apart
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is a mule sterile?
items.correct: Because it has 63 chromosomes, 32 from the horse and 31 from the donkey, which are not homologous pairs and cannot all pair up in meiosis, so viable gametes are not formed.
items.misconception: A mule is sterile because a hybrid is an unnatural, weak or unhealthy mixture whose body cannot function properly.
items.why: 'Hybrid' and 'mixture' suggest something defective, and students reason that anything nature 'does not intend' must be sickly, although mules are in fact strong and long-lived. Hybrid sterility is a failure of meiosis, not of health. The mule's odd number of chromosomes, inherited from parents with 64 and 62, cannot form homologous pairs, so it cannot produce functional gametes even though it is a vigorous animal.
items.specStatementText: Barriers and sterile hybrids keep gene pools apart
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would a plant with double the normal number of chromosomes survive?
items.correct: Yes. Polyploidy is common in plants and polyploid plants are usually healthy; a doubled hybrid gains fertility because every chromosome has a homologous partner for meiosis.
items.misconception: Having extra sets of chromosomes is harmful or lethal, as an extra chromosome is in humans, so a polyploid plant would not survive.
items.why: The only examples of abnormal chromosome number most students have met are human conditions such as Down syndrome, so any departure from the diploid number is expected to be damaging. In plants, polyploidy is frequent and well tolerated. Whole extra sets of chromosomes are balanced, unlike a single extra chromosome, and doubling the chromosome number of a sterile hybrid restores fertility because the chromosomes can pair in meiosis.
items.specStatementText: Plants can form new species in one generation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a new polyploid plant species still interbreed with its parent species?
items.correct: No, not to produce fertile offspring. Crossing the polyploid with a parent species gives offspring with an unbalanced chromosome number that cannot pair in meiosis, so the polyploid is reproductively isolated from both parents.
items.misconception: A polyploid plant is still the same species as its parents, because it looks similar and can still breed with them.
items.why: Species are judged by appearance, and the polyploid looks much like its parents, so students assume interbreeding continues and no new species has formed. The polyploid produces gametes with a different chromosome number from those of either parent species, so crosses with the parents give sterile offspring. It is reproductively isolated from both, which makes it a new species from the moment it forms.
items.specStatementText: Plants can form new species in one generation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If one individual is born with a mutation that makes it very different, is it a new species?
items.correct: No. Speciation is the splitting of a population into groups that can no longer interbreed; a single mutant individual is still a member of its parents' species and can breed with them.
items.misconception: A new species begins when a single individual is born with a large mutation that makes it different from the rest.
items.why: Mutation is taught as the source of new alleles, and fiction shows 'mutants' as new kinds of creature, so students place speciation in one individual rather than in the divergence of populations. Speciation happens to populations: new species have appeared only by the splitting of pre-existing species into groups that become reproductively isolated. A mutation in one individual changes that individual's alleles but does not create a species.
items.specStatementText: New species only ever come from splitting old ones
